title: Zoya's Digital Garden Blight
markdown:
Zoya’s holographic garden had never needed a weather report. Lately a peculiar dullness crept across the flora all the same. Some plants wilted into grey wisps. Others, right beside them, stayed vivid. She analysed the digital soil, tweaked light frequencies, and muttered encouragement at an orchid that had no ears. Nothing stopped the gloom. A tremor of worry. Unseen forces. A creeping silence stealing the light.

“It’s like a wilting whisper, Pebble,” she said, watching the orchid droop.

Pebble, her ancient tortoise, blinked slowly. “Hmph,” he offered, a deep sympathetic sound that had served him for decades.

“I don’t understand how it’s moving. It’s not as if they have little legs to spread their sadness.”

Ms. Lin, neighbour and teacher, popped her head in, a smile crinkling her eyes. “Still wrestling the digital doldrums?” She held up a sleek device. “A game, then. Sometimes the simplest play shows the path.”

They sat around a simulation. “Epidemic Escape,” Lin said. “These dots are plants. Some are feeling poorly.” Bright green for healthy. Dusty grey for droop. Zoya watched the grey dots nudge the green ones. Slowly those greens turned dusty too, colour draining. The screen filled with a silent tide of grey.

“See?” Lin said softly. “The blight travels from one to the next. A chain. Like falling dominoes.”

Zoya leaned closer, breath catching. “A ripple. When one is affected, it touches its neighbours. It spreads along connections. If we could stop it touching so many at once…” A new idea, bright as a firefly. “What if we made space between the sick and the healthy? A hedge. A buffer of green.”

Lin beamed. “You’re seeing the links.”

Zoya hurried back to the garden. She did not need to cure every sick plant; that looked impossible on this clock. She needed to slow the journey. The wilting started from a few specific digital shrubs.

“These are the first ones.” A few deft clicks isolated them into a quarantined corner, a grey little island with a hard border. Then she moved her strongest ferns and succulents into a verdant wall between the sick shrubs and the rest. A few plants showing the faintest hint of grey got their own space, not quite condemned, not quite trusted.

She sat with Pebble while the simulation ticked overnight in a side window, a smaller echo of the same rules. He fell asleep mid-hmph. She did not.

The next morning she held her breath as the garden loaded. The grey wisps still clung to the quarantined shrubs. The healthy plants, shielded by ferns and succulents, were still vividly green. Relief, like the first cool dew.

“It worked.”

Lin nodded. She did not compare the forest’s growth or hidden pathways of the universe. “Transmission chains. Something spreads from one to another. Break the contact, and the rest can keep their colour.”

Zoya looked at Pebble, who gave a slow approving blink. She exported the buffer layout, labelled the quarantine folder so she would not drag it back by accident, and watered the healthy beds with a light cycle that was only a little celebratory. She did not ask what other patterns the world was hiding. She watched one grey shrub on the island put out a tentative new frond, still pale, and left it there, apart, until it earned its way home.
